questions.q: According to this lesson, what should legitimately differ between dev, test, and production environments?
options: The intensity of governance controls, not whether governance principles apply at all
Nothing -- every environment must have byte-for-byte identical configuration
Only production needs any governance; dev and test can be left ungoverned
Only naming conventions, since security controls are irrelevant outside production
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that sandbox, dev, test, and prod should inherit from the same landing-zone pattern -- what legitimately differs is intensity (e.g. looser convenience restrictions in dev), never whether core guardrails like encryption apply.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call treating "non-production" as a synonym for "ungoverned" a costly mistake?
options: Because real customer data regularly ends up in dev or test environments through copies, debugging, and exports
Because non-production environments never contain any data worth protecting
Because cloud providers automatically apply production-grade security to every environment regardless of labeling
Because dev and test environments are technically incapable of experiencing data breaches
questions.explain: Dev and test environments frequently end up holding real customer data via database copies, debugging sessions, or sample exports -- weak access control there is just as much a breach as the same gap in production.

options: Drift caused by a one-off manual change -- like loosening a network rule to debug something -- that never gets reverted
Drift that only occurs when a cloud provider changes its service pricing
Drift caused exclusively by automated deployment pipelines, never by a person
A type of drift that only affects identity and access management, never networking or storage
questions.explain: Manual override drift happens when someone with sufficient permissions makes a direct one-off change -- to debug something, silence a noisy alert -- and never reverts it, so the resource quietly diverges from its intended governed state.

options: Drift that happens when a new resource type or deployment pattern isn't covered by existing policy, so it deploys technically compliant while violating the policy's intent
Drift caused by a cloud provider's outage or service disruption
Drift that only happens in sandbox environments, never in production
The same thing as manual override drift, just under a different name
questions.explain: Policy gap drift is a distinct cause: policy wasn't written to anticipate a new resource type or pattern, so the resource can satisfy the letter of existing policy while still violating its intent.

questions.q: What do Azure Policy and AWS Config have in common, as described in this lesson?
options: Both continuously evaluate resources against their expected configuration and make drift visible, without preventing it by themselves
Both are identity providers used to authenticate users into the cloud console
Both are billing tools with no connection to governance or compliance
Both automatically delete any resource that drifts out of compliance
questions.explain: Azure Policy reports ongoing compliance state and AWS Config evaluates configuration history against Config rules -- both make drift visible on an ongoing basis, which the lesson calls the precondition for fixing it, though neither prevents drift by itself (that's Chapter 4's preventive controls).
